# Gasses Gasses are a critical part of the station's operation. You may know them as the stuff you breathe, but they are also used in many other ways.
Gasses have certain properties that make them useful for different tasks. Atmospherics can also synthesize exotic gasses from other gasses, which can be used for special purposes. Additionally, any gas may be produced by a plant with the correct mutations.
## Oxygen
A common gas, used by most species on the station to breathe.
Oxygen is an oxidizer, which means it supports combustion. This makes it both useful when fusing gasses in a burn chamber, and dangerous when mixed with flammable gasses.
## Nitrogen
An inert gas, used in part with oxygen to create a breathable atmosphere.
Nitrogen is very stable and comprises most of a standard breathable atmosphere.
Some species like Slimes breathe nitrogen, with the Vox species requiring strictly nitrogen to breathe.
## Air Mix
A mixture of gasses that is breathable to most species on the station. It consists of 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen.
## Carbon Dioxide
A waste gas produced by most species on the station. A common byproduct of combustion.
Despite seeming useless, some departments use it in their line of work.
## Water Vapor
A common gas, produced by the burning of plasma and other processes.
Water vapor has a good specific heat capacity compared to other gasses, making it useful for moving heat around.
## Plasma
A highly flammable gas that is used in many processes on the station.
Engineering uses this gas to generate power and create exotic gasses.
Burning it generates a lot of heat, as well as gas byproducts such as carbon dioxide, water vapor, and tritium, depending on the efficiency of the burn.
Plasma gas also has a good specific heat capacity, making it useful for moving heat around.
## Tritium
An extremely flammable radioactive gas that is used in the creation of frezon.
Tritium is produced when burning plasma in a burn chamber, and can be used to create frezon gas in a complicated mixing process.
The efficiency of tritium fusion depends on various factors such as burn richness and temperature.
## Frezon
A highly sought after gas, due to the difficulty in creating it and its many properties.
It has an extremely high specific heat capacity, making it excellent for moving large amounts of heat around.
Frezon can combine in the air with nitrogen to create nitrous oxide, alongside cooling down the air significantly to below freezing temperatures.
Frezon is very complicated to create, requiring a mix of tritium, oxygen, and nitrogen, all tuned precisely to create the gas. If you're looking to create this gas yourself, here's what you need to know: - Frezon is produced by the combination of oxygen, tritium, and nitrogen. - Tritium and oxygen are mixed at a ratio of around 1:8. - Nitrogen is required as a catalyst for the reaction. The amount of nitrogen consumed is dependent on the efficiency of the reaction. - The frezon reaction only occurs at cryogenic temperatures, below 73.15 K. The efficency of the reaction (how much frezon is produced) is dependent on the temperature. The closer to 73.15 K, the more frezon is produced, and the less nitrogen is consumed.
Remember, atmospherics is all about experimentation and process optimization. Try it until you get it right!
## Nitrous Oxide
A recreational and waste gas, produced by slimes and the combination of frezon and nitrogen.
## Ammonia
A gas produced by the decomposition of bodies. If inhaled, causes poisoning and vomiting.
Can be condensed to create ammonia, which can be used to make space cleaner.
## Methane
A poisonous, flammable, orange-brown gas. Burns begin at 100C and scales linearly to 1370C. Consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water vapour in a ratio of 1:2:1:2 (CH4:O2:CO2:H2O). Releases 3.5x as much energy as plasma per mole of gas.
Can be synthesised by mixing carbon dioxide and hydrogen in a ratio of 1:4, as long as the temperature is less than 600K and pressure is above 2MPa.
## Hydrogen
A flammable, slightly poisonous, colourless gas. Burns begin at 100C and scales linearly to 1370C. Consumes oxygen and produces water vapour in a ratio of 2:1:2(H2:O2:H2O). Releases ~1.75x as much energy as plasma per mole of gas.
## Chlorine
A poisonous yellow gas. Limited usage outside of chemistry.
## Fluorine
A poisonous yellow-green gas. Causes chemical burns when inhaled.
## Chlorine Trifluoride
A red gas that should be avoided.

It is hypergolic with every known fuel, and so rapidly hypergolic that no ignition delay has ever been measured. It is also hypergolic with such things as cloth, wood, and test engineers, not to mention asbestos, sand, and water—with which it reacts explosively. It can be kept in some of the ordinary structural metals—steel, copper, aluminum, etc.—because of the formation of a thin film of insoluble metal fluoride that protects the bulk of the metal, just as the invisible coat of oxide on aluminium keeps it from burning up in the atmosphere. If, however, this coat is melted or scrubbed off, and has no chance to reform, the operator is confronted with the problem of coping with a metal-fluorine fire. Material science has advanced in the last two and a half centuries, but ClF3 is still extremely dangerous. Notable advances include walls and clothes that do not react, though you are not your clothes and still burn unless all skin is completely covered by a hardsuit.
Fires involving ClF3 do not use oxygen, and instead react with any of tritium, water vapor, hydrogen, ammonia, methane and plasma. They reach maximum burn rate at 300C, which is much lower than other flammable gases. If tritium is in the fire, it burns much more violently and also produces radiation. It produces chlorine and fluorine regardless of what it's burning with, and may produce nitrrogen, carbon dioxide or hydrogen depending on other gasses in the mix. Most burns release 2.5x the amount of energy compared to plasma, with tritium instead releasing 12.5x.
The first step for producing it is to reconsider. After that, source chlorine and fluorine in the ratio 1:3:2 (Cl2:F2:ClF3), and mix at or above 250C. Releases approximately the same amount of heat as a plasfire (per mole ClF3 formed/plasma burnt).
